title: English Vocabulary 3 · Units 29–30
description: Curated B2 vocabulary and usage for medicine and technology, nutrition, and health and lifestyle, with independently written examples and Brazilian Portuguese glosses.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets and topic coverage were reviewed against the source and exercise answer key; all explanatory notes and example sentences are newly written. Original exercises and extended book passages are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Full study pages, medical-device illustrations, food tables, grammar and language-help notes, exercises and relevant answer-key entries checked for lexical and grammatical coverage.
audit.pronunciation: Selected broad British IPA for high-confidence words and short expressions; uncertain or long transcriptions are left blank. Connected-speech and regional variants are not exhaustively described.
audit.languagePolicy: All fields are in English except Brazilian Portuguese translations in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Manual review of study pages and illustrations, exercises and answer key; lexical and original-example review; audio target and offline JSON schema, provenance and duplicate-ID validation. No live application or browser TTS/recognition tests were performed.
audit.limitations: No prerecorded audio is included. Browser TTS, speech recognition and an actual VocabLab import have not been tested. Health claims from the textbook are presented as language examples and not independently medically validated.

units.title: Unit 29 — Medicine and technology
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 29. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Describe historic and modern medical technologies and the functions of common medical devices.
Use natural collocations to discuss advances, medical diagnosis and disease treatment.
Distinguish technical meanings and use operate on correctly when discussing surgery.

items.example: Medical technology has changed how hospitals diagnose illness.
items.note: Equipment and techniques designed to prevent, diagnose or treat medical conditions.

items.example: After injuring his knee, he needed crutches for several weeks.
items.note: Usually plural; a crutch is a support used when walking.

items.example: He put on his spectacles to read the small print.
items.note: A more formal or old-fashioned British term for glasses; normally plural.

items.example: I need my glasses to read the timetable.
items.note: Eyewear is normally referred to in the plural; one pair of glasses.

items.example: Regular eye tests can detect changes in your vision.
items.note: Here, vision means the ability to see.

items.example: These lenses help correct vision at different distances.
items.note: Correct means improve or remedy a sight problem in this context.

items.example: The theatre provides wheelchair access at the side entrance.
items.note: A chair with wheels designed for someone who has difficulty walking.

items.example: The surgeon explained why a general anaesthetic was necessary.
items.note: British spelling anaesthetic; it makes a patient unconscious during an operation.

items.example: The doctor requested an X-ray of my wrist.
items.note: Can refer to the radiation or an image made using it; plural X-rays.

items.example: X-ray equipment uses radiation to produce diagnostic images.
items.note: Energy transmitted as waves or particles; medical use requires careful control.

items.example: She wears a contact lens in each eye when playing sport.
items.note: Often plural: contact lenses; placed directly on the surface of the eye.

items.example: The company manufactures precision parts for medical devices.
items.note: Produce goods, typically in large numbers in a factory.

items.example: Researchers continue to make rapid advances in medical imaging.
items.note: The standard collocation is make advances in an area.

items.example: A recent advance has improved the accuracy of the scanner.
items.note: As a noun, an improvement or new development.

items.example: Many treatments have changed over the past decade.
items.note: A period of ten years.

items.example: Hospitals use a vast range of monitoring equipment.
items.note: Vast emphasises that the variety is very large.

items.example: This small device measures the patient's pulse.
items.note: Equipment designed for a particular function.

items.example: The clinic installed a sophisticated imaging system.
items.note: Highly developed or technologically complex.

items.example: The device helps people with hearing difficulties follow conversations.
items.note: Difficulties with hearing is another natural phrasing.

items.example: Her hearing aid connects wirelessly to her phone.
items.note: A device that improves hearing by amplifying or processing sound.

items.example: The patient received a pacemaker to regulate his heartbeat.
items.note: An implanted electronic device that helps control heart rhythm.

items.example: The patient now walks comfortably with an artificial joint.
items.note: Made by humans rather than occurring naturally.

items.example: She received an artificial hip after the old joint wore out.
items.note: An artificial replacement for the natural hip joint.

items.example: An artificial knee can help restore mobility after joint damage.
items.note: A manufactured replacement for the knee joint.

items.example: He had pain in his left hip after the fall.
items.note: The area or joint where the leg meets the pelvis.

items.example: The new system is highly efficient at processing medical images.
items.note: Highly is a common intensifier with efficient.

items.example: The athlete trained with a lightweight prosthetic leg.
items.note: Prosthetic describes an artificial replacement for a missing body part.

items.example: A robotic arm can assist a patient with everyday tasks.
items.note: A mechanically controlled arm; not necessarily a prosthetic limb.

items.example: The new gripper can pick things up without damaging them.
items.note: Pick up is a separable phrasal verb: pick the cup up.

items.example: He wears reading glasses because his eyesight has changed.
items.note: Close in meaning to vision; refers to how well a person sees.

items.example: She asked about laser surgery for her vision problem.
items.note: Surgery that uses a focused beam of light.

items.pt: escâner; aparelho de diagnóstico por imagem
items.example: The hospital bought a new scanner for detailed examinations.
items.note: An electronic instrument used to examine or produce images of the body.

items.example: Early tests may help doctors identify a disease before symptoms worsen.
items.note: Identify means recognise what something is; it does not necessarily mean cure.

items.pt: em estágio inicial; numa fase inicial
items.example: The team detected the fault at an early stage.
items.note: Use at an early stage of a process or illness.

items.example: The doctor needed more information to diagnose the illness.
items.note: Diagnose means determine the nature of a medical problem, not merely notice it.

items.example: The specialist confirmed the diagnosis after further tests.
items.note: Noun associated with diagnose; plural diagnoses.

items.example: A specialist reviewed the scan from a distance.
items.note: Emphasises not being physically present at the patient's location.

items.example: The patient described her symptoms to the nurse.
items.note: A person receiving medical assessment or treatment.

items.example: A persistent cough can be a symptom of several illnesses.
items.note: A sign or experience suggesting a health problem.

items.example: The monitor automatically records each measurement.
items.note: Without requiring a person to perform each individual step.

items.example: The nurse checked his blood pressure before the consultation.
items.note: The pressure of circulating blood in the arteries.

items.example: The device can record body temperature every minute.
items.note: A measure of how warm the body is.

items.example: We used a digital thermometer to check her temperature.
items.note: An instrument for measuring temperature.

items.example: The research team stored anonymous results in a database.
items.note: An organised collection of information; plural databases.

items.example: The medication is used to treat a disease affecting the lungs.
items.note: Treat means provide care or intervention; it does not guarantee a cure.

items.example: Researchers hope to find ways to cure the illness.
items.note: Cure implies eliminating the illness, unlike manage or treat.

items.pt: ferramentas médicas; recursos para a medicina
items.example: Doctors use a variety of medical tools to investigate symptoms.
items.note: Tools can include instruments, techniques or information resources.

items.pt: cirurgia minimamente invasiva; cirurgia por pequenas incisões
items.example: The surgeon discussed whether keyhole surgery would be suitable.
items.note: Surgery performed through small openings, often using a camera and special instruments.

items.example: The surgeon will operate on the patient tomorrow.
items.note: In this meaning, operate normally requires on before the person or body part.

items.example: The sports centre offers accessible facilities for disabled athletes.
items.note: Refers to people with disabilities; follow a person's preferred terminology where known.

items.example: The event included both disabled and able-bodied competitors.
items.note: Describes people who do not have a physical disability.

items.example: The physiotherapist assessed the patient's mobility.
items.note: The ability to move around freely or easily.

sectionsChecked: A: Historical equipment, vision and manufacturing vocabulary, with illustrated chronology
B: Modern medical devices, prosthetics and collocations for technological advances
C: Diagnosis, patient monitoring, healthcare data and surgical techniques
Exercises 29.1–29.4 and answer-key vocabulary, including objects shown in the exercise figures

units.title: Unit 30 — Health and lifestyle
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 30. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Describe diet, nutrition and health using accurate upper-intermediate collocations.
Distinguish related forms such as obese/obesity, stress/stressful and fit/fitness.
Use correct countability with food, foods, fruit, fruits and fish, and describe lifestyle changes.

items.example: A balanced diet includes different types of food.
items.note: Diet may mean habitual eating patterns, not necessarily a weight-loss plan.

items.example: Scientists are studying the long-term effects of the treatment.
items.note: Describes something lasting or affecting a long period.

items.example: People who consume large amounts of sugar may need to review their diet.
items.note: More formal than eat or drink.

items.example: The factory purchases raw materials in large quantities.
items.note: A quantity is an amount; this phrase also applies to food and drink.

items.pt: peixe gorduroso; peixe rico em óleo
items.example: Salmon is an example of oily fish.
items.note: Fish with relatively high amounts of oil in their tissues.

items.example: We baked salmon with lemon and herbs.
items.note: The letter l is silent; salmon has the same form in many plural uses.

items.example: Sugary foods can contribute a great deal of sugar to the diet.
items.note: Sugary means containing a lot of sugar.

items.example: They replaced some fizzy drinks with water.
items.note: British English; fizzy means containing gas bubbles.

items.example: The label shows that the product has a high fat content.
items.note: Fat content refers to the amount of fat in food.

items.example: We compared two soups with different salt content.
items.note: Common pattern: a high/low salt content.

items.example: The shop sells fresh ingredients alongside processed foods.
items.note: Foods altered through industrial or other processing; the health effect depends on the product.

items.example: She makes her sandwiches with wholemeal bread.
items.note: British English; made with flour containing the whole grain.

items.example: Fresh fruit is available in the staff kitchen.
items.note: Usually uncountable when talking about fruit generally.

items.example: A small packet of nuts makes a convenient snack.
items.note: In this unit, nuts are edible seeds or hard-shelled fruits.

items.example: The label calls the berries a superfood.
items.note: A popular marketing term, not a precise scientific category.

items.example: Vaccination can help prevent disease in a community.
items.note: Prevent means stop something from happening.

items.example: The organisation offers support for employees' mental health.
items.note: Health related to psychological and emotional wellbeing.

items.example: Regular movement can support physical health.
items.note: Refers to the state of the body, in contrast with mental health.

items.example: She added blueberries to her breakfast.
items.note: Small edible blue fruits; the singular is blueberry.

items.example: The researcher designed a task to assess short-term memory.
items.note: The capacity to retain information briefly.

items.example: Researchers are investigating ways to slow the ageing process.
items.note: The verb slow means make a process proceed more gradually; no single food guarantees this effect.

items.example: The ageing process affects people in different ways.
items.note: British spelling ageing; American English often aging.

items.example: Oranges are a familiar source of vitamin C.
items.note: Common construction: a good source of a nutrient.

items.example: The clinician suggested changes that might help lower cholesterol.
items.note: Lower means reduce a level or amount.

items.example: The doctor ordered a test to check her cholesterol.
items.note: A fatty substance in the body, often measured in blood tests.

items.example: We added spinach to the vegetable soup.
items.note: An edible leafy vegetable.

items.example: The nutritional label says the product is high in vitamin A.
items.note: High in describes having a relatively large amount of a nutrient.

items.example: The article claims the supplement could boost the immune system.
items.note: Boost means increase or improve; medical claims require evidence.

items.example: The immune system helps the body respond to infections.
items.note: The body's network of cells, tissues and mechanisms for defence.

items.pt: suco de vegetais; suco de legumes
items.example: The café serves fresh vegetable juice at lunchtime.
items.note: A drink made by extracting liquid from vegetables.

items.example: Wearing a seat belt can reduce the risk of injury.
items.note: Common pattern: reduce the risk of something happening.

items.example: The report discusses ways to reduce the risk of heart disease.
items.note: A broad term for conditions affecting the heart.

items.example: The survey revealed a sharp rise in transport costs.
items.note: Sharp describes a sudden, large increase; rise is a noun here.

items.example: The report compared health outcomes among adults classified as obese.
items.note: Medical adjective; can sound judgemental when used to describe a person, so context matters.

items.example: The research examines social and biological factors related to obesity.
items.note: Noun related to obese.

items.example: The programme addresses childhood obesity through several approaches.
items.note: Obesity occurring during childhood.

items.example: The water leak became a major problem for the building.
items.note: Major means important or serious.

items.example: He tries to take exercise during his lunch break.
items.note: A British English expression for being physically active.

items.example: Many people find it easier to get regular exercise with a routine.
items.note: Use get or take exercise; exercise is uncountable for activity in general.

items.example: She cycles to work to keep fit.
items.note: Informal, natural expression meaning remain in good physical condition.

items.example: Swimming helps him maintain fitness throughout the year.
items.note: Maintain means keep something at a particular standard or level.

items.example: The trainer assessed their fitness at the start of the programme.
items.note: Fitness is a noun; fit is an adjective.

items.example: The move to a new office was stressful for the entire team.
items.note: Describes a situation that causes stress.

items.example: Heavy workloads can cause stress.
items.note: A noun or verb; contrast the noun stress with the adjective stressful.

items.example: The nurse advised him to monitor his high blood pressure.
items.note: A long-term elevation in blood pressure is often called hypertension.

items.example: The emergency team treated a patient who had suffered a heart attack.
items.note: A medical emergency in which blood supply to part of the heart is blocked.

items.example: The report examined the relationship between depression and sleep.
items.note: In health contexts, a condition affecting mood and functioning, not simply momentary sadness.

items.example: Going to bed very late became a bad habit.
items.note: A repeated behaviour that causes problems.

items.example: Improper handling of chemicals can cause serious harm.
items.note: Harm is an uncountable noun meaning injury or damage.

items.example: The fumes may be harmful if inhaled.
items.note: Harmful is an adjective; harm is a noun or verb.

items.example: The public-health campaign describes the risks of tobacco use.
items.note: The plant material used in cigarettes and other tobacco products.

items.example: The label shows the alcohol content of the drink.
items.note: Uncountable for alcohol generally; alcoholic drinks are countable.

items.example: He exercises regularly by walking and swimming.
items.note: Exercise can be an intransitive verb; regularly is an adverb.

items.example: The study included participants who suffer from obesity.
items.note: Use suffer from with a condition; in person-centred language, have obesity may be preferred.

items.pt: tipos de alimento; alimentos de diferentes variedades
items.example: The market sells foods from many different countries.
items.note: Plural foods often means types or varieties; food is generally uncountable.

items.example: The stall sells tropical fruits that are hard to find elsewhere.
items.note: Fruits often refers to kinds; fruit is more usual for fruit in general.

items.example: Several fish were swimming near the rocks.
items.note: For ordinary plurals, fish remains fish; fishes is chiefly used for separate species or specialised contexts.

items.example: The study explored the possible health benefits of walking.
items.note: A health benefit is a positive effect on health; avoid assuming that every claimed benefit is proven.

items.example: She brought a healthy snack for the train journey.
items.note: An adjective + noun collocation used for food eaten between meals.

items.example: There was a noticeable rise in attendance this year.
items.note: Rise is an intransitive verb or a noun; it is not interchangeable with transitive raise.

items.example: The company decided to raise the subscription price.
items.note: Raise normally requires an object; compare prices rise with raise prices.

sectionsChecked: A: Food categories, nutrient collocations, the superfood text and usage distinctions
B: Fitness, obesity, stress, harm and related noun-adjective expressions
Language help: countable and uncountable food, fruit and fish
Exercises 30.1–30.6, collocation and common-error prompts and answer key
